{{DISPLAYTITLE:''In silico'' clinical trials}}
An '''''in silico'' clinical trial''', also known as a virtual clinical trial, is an individualized [[computer simulation]] used in the development or regulatory evaluation of a [[medicinal product]], [[medical device|device]], or intervention. While completely simulated [[clinical trial]]s are not feasible with current technology and understanding of biology, its development would be expected to have major benefits over current ''[[in vivo]]'' clinical trials, and research on it is being pursued.

== History ==
The term ''in silico'' indicates any use of computers in clinical trials, even if limited to management of clinical information in a database.<ref>This sense of the term was used in 2011 in a position paper from the VPH Institute commenting on the [[green paper]] written ahead of the launch of the [[European Commission]] [[Horizon 2020]] framework programme.

[http://www.vph-institute.org/upload/vphinst-position-on-fp8-greenpaper-v3_5192443874603.pdf VPH greenpaper]</ref>

== Rationale ==
The traditional model for the development of medical treatments and devices begins with [[pre-clinical development]]. In laboratories, test-tube and other ''[[in vitro]]'' experiments establish the plausibility for the efficacy of the treatment.  Then ''[[in vivo]]'' [[animal models]], with different species, provide guidance on the efficacy and safety of the product for humans. With success in both ''in vitro'' and ''in vivo'' studies, scientists can propose that clinical trials test whether the product should be made available for humans. Clinical trials are often divided into four phases. Phase 3  involves testing a large number of people.<ref name="Trial Watch">{{cite journal | vauthors = Arrowsmith J, Miller P | title = Trial watch: phase II and phase III attrition rates 2011-2012 | journal = Nature Reviews. Drug Discovery | volume = 12 | issue = 8 | page = 569 | date = August 2013 | pmid = 23903212 | doi = 10.1038/nrd4090 | doi-access = free }}</ref> When a medication fails at this stage, the financial losses can be catastrophic.<ref name="Model-Based Drug Development">{{cite journal | vauthors = Milligan PA, Brown MJ, Marchant B, Martin SW, van der Graaf PH, Benson N, Nucci G, Nichols DJ, Boyd RA, Mandema JW, Krishnaswami S, Zwillich S, Gruben D, Anziano RJ, Stock TC, Lalonde RL | display-authors = 6 | title = Model-based drug development: a rational approach to efficiently accelerate drug development | journal = Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics | volume = 93 | issue = 6 | pages = 502–514 | date = June 2013 | pmid = 23588322 | doi = 10.1038/clpt.2013.54 | s2cid = 29806156 }}</ref>

Predicting low-frequency side effects has been difficult, because such side effects need not become apparent until the treatment is adopted by many patients. The appearance of severe side-effects in phase three often causes development to stop, for ethical and economic reasons.<ref name="Trial Watch" /><ref name="Modeling and Similation as a tool. Harnisch">{{cite journal | vauthors = Harnisch L, Shepard T, Pons G, Della Pasqua O | title = Modeling and simulation as a tool to bridge efficacy and safety data in special populations | journal =   CPT: Pharmacometrics & Systems Pharmacology| volume = 2 | issue = 2 | pages = e28 | date = February 2013 | pmid = 23835939 | pmc = 3600759 | doi = 10.1038/psp.2013.6 }}</ref><ref name="canine cardiac midmyocardial model">{{cite journal | vauthors = Davies MR, Mistry HB, Hussein L, Pollard CE, Valentin JP, Swinton J, Abi-Gerges N | title = An in silico canine cardiac midmyocardial action potential duration model as a tool for early drug safety assessment | journal = American Journal of Physiology. Heart and Circulatory Physiology | volume = 302 | issue = 7 | pages = H1466–H1480 | date = April 2012 | pmid = 22198175 | doi = 10.1152/ajpheart.00808.2011 }}</ref> Also, in recent years many candidate drugs failed in phase 3 trials because of lack of efficacy rather than for safety reasons.<ref name="Trial Watch" /><ref name="Model-Based Drug Development" /> One reason for failure is that traditional trials aim to establish efficacy and safety for most subjects, rather than for individual subjects, and so efficacy is determined by a [[statistic]] of [[central tendency]] for the trial. Traditional trials do not adapt the treatment to the [[covariate]]s of subjects:
* Taking account of factors such as the patient's particular physiology, the individual manifestation of the disease being treated, their lifestyle, and the presence of co-morbidities.<ref name="Modeling and Similation as a tool. Harnisch" /><ref name="A Vision and Strategy for VPH. Hunter et al.">{{cite journal | vauthors = Hunter P, Chapman T, Coveney PV, de Bono B, Diaz V, Fenner J, Frangi AF, Harris P, Hose R, Kohl P, Lawford P, McCormack K, Mendes M, Omholt S, Quarteroni A, Shublaq N, Skår J, Stroetmann K, Tegner J, Thomas SR, Tollis I, Tsamardinos I, van Beek JH, Viceconti M | display-authors = 6 | title = A vision and strategy for the virtual physiological human: 2012 update | journal = Interface Focus | volume = 3 | issue = 2 | article-number = 20130004 | date = April 2013 | pmid = 24427536 | pmc = 3638492 | doi = 10.1098/rsfs.2013.0004 }}</ref>
* [[Compliance (medicine)|Compliance]], or lack thereof, in taking the drug at the times and dose prescribed. In the case of a surgically implanted device, to account for the variability in surgeons' experience and technique, as well as the particular anatomy of the patient.<ref name="Pre-clinical validation of joint prostheses. Viceconti">{{cite journal | vauthors = Viceconti M, Affatato S, Baleani M, Bordini B, Cristofolini L, Taddei F | title = Pre-clinical validation of joint prostheses: a systematic approach | journal = Journal of the Mechanical Behavior of Biomedical Materials | volume = 2 | issue = 1 | pages = 120–127 | date = January 2009 | pmid = 19627814 | doi = 10.1016/j.jmbbm.2008.02.005 }}</ref> However, adjusting the evaluation of the study for noncompliance has proved difficult. Such adjustments often bias the results of the study, and so many health authorities mandate that clinical trials analyse the data according to the [[intention to treat]] principle.

== Aim ==
Accurate computer models of a treatment and its deployment, as well as patient characteristics, are necessary precursors for the development of ''in silico'' clinical trials.The [[European Medicines Agency]] (EMA) and the U.S. FDA have both issued guidance supporting the use of modeling, simulation, and [[virtual patient]] populations to inform regulatory decisions in drug and medical device development.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Manolis E, Rohou S, Hemmings R, Salmonson T, Karlsson M, Milligan PA |title=The Role of Modeling and Simulation in Development and Registration of Medicinal Products |journal=CPT: Pharmacometrics & Systems Pharmacology |year=2013 |volume=2 |issue=2 |pages=e31 |doi=10.1038/psp.2013.7|pmc=3600760 }}</ref>
<ref name="canine cardiac midmyocardial model" /><ref name="A Vision and Strategy for VPH. Hunter et al." /><ref name="Grand Challenge: Applying Regulatory Science and Big Data to Improve Medical Device Innovation. Erdman">{{cite journal | vauthors = Erdman AG, Keefe DF, Schiestl R | title = Grand challenge: applying regulatory science and big data to improve medical device innovation | journal = IEEE Transactions on Bio-Medical Engineering | volume = 60 | issue = 3 | pages = 700–706 | date = March 2013 | pmid = 23380845 | doi = 10.1109/TBME.2013.2244600 | bibcode = 2013ITBE...60..700E | s2cid = 442791 }}</ref><ref name="In silico design of clinical trials.Clermont">{{cite journal | vauthors = Clermont G, Bartels J, Kumar R, Constantine G, Vodovotz Y, Chow C | title = In silico design of clinical trials: a method coming of age | journal = Critical Care Medicine | volume = 32 | issue = 10 | pages = 2061–2070 | date = October 2004 | pmid = 15483415 | doi = 10.1097/01.CCM.0000142394.28791.C3 | s2cid = 10952248 }}</ref>  In such a scenario, 'virtual' patients would be given a 'virtual' treatment, enabling observation through a computer simulation of how the candidate biomedical product performs and whether it produces the intended effect, without inducing adverse effects.  Such ''in silico'' clinical trials could help to reduce, refine, and partially replace real clinical trials by:
* Reducing the size and the duration of clinical trials through better design,<ref name="A Vision and Strategy for VPH. Hunter et al." /><ref name="Grand Challenge: Applying Regulatory Science and Big Data to Improve Medical Device Innovation. Erdman" /> for example, by identifying characteristics to determine which patients might be at greater risk of complications or providing earlier confirmation that the product<ref name="canine cardiac midmyocardial model" /> or process<ref name="insilco Schizophrenia ">{{cite web | title=New Technological Breakthroughs for Patient-Specific Healthcare and Schizophrenia |  vauthors = Agarwal Y | website=ETHealthworld.com | date=2019-02-15 | url=https://health.economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/industry/new-technological-breakthroughs-for-patient-specific-healthcare-and-schizophrenia/68012036 | access-date=2019-04-01}}</ref> is working as expected.
* Refining clinical trials through clearer, more detailed information on potential outcomes and greater [[explanatory power]] in interpreting any adverse effects that might emerge, as well as better understanding of how the tested product interacts with the individual patient anatomy and predicting long-term or rare effects that clinical trials are unlikely to reveal.<ref name="In silico design of clinical trials.Clermont" />
* Partially replacing clinical trials in those situations where it is not an absolute regulatory necessity, but only a legal requirement. There are already examples where regulators have accepted the replacement of animal models with ''in silico'' models under appropriate conditions.<ref name="In silico preclinical trials: a proof of concept in closed-loop control of type 1 diabetes. Kovatchev">{{cite journal | vauthors = Kovatchev BP, Breton M, Man CD, Cobelli C | title = In silico preclinical trials: a proof of concept in closed-loop control of type 1 diabetes | journal = Journal of Diabetes Science and Technology | volume = 3 | issue = 1 | pages = 44–55 | date = January 2009 | pmid = 19444330 | pmc = 2681269 | doi = 10.1177/193229680900300106 }}</ref> While real clinical trials will remain essential in most cases, there are specific situations where a reliable predictive model can conceivably replace a routine clinical assessment.
In addition, real clinical trials may indicate that a product is unsafe or ineffective, but rarely indicate why or suggest how it might be improved. As such, a product that fails during clinical trials may simply be abandoned, even if a small modification would solve the problem. This stifles innovation, decreasing the number of truly original biomedical products presented to the market every year, and at the same time increasing the cost of development.<ref name="Avicenna Roadmap 2015 Viceconti">{{cite web | vauthors = Viceconti M, Morley-Fletcher E, Henney A, Contin M, El-Arifi K, McGregor C, Karlstrom A, Wilkinson E |title = In Silico Clinical Trials: How Computer Simulation Will Transform The Biomedical Industry An international research and development roadmap for an industry-driven initiative|url = http://avicenna-isct.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/05/Avicenna_roadmap_v3.pdf|website = Avicenna-ISCT|publisher = Avicenna Project|access-date = 1 June 2015|ref = AvicennaRoadmap}}</ref>
Analysis through ''in silico'' clinical trials is expected to provide a better understanding of the mechanism that caused the product to fail in testing,<ref name="Grand Challenge: Applying Regulatory Science and Big Data to Improve Medical Device Innovation. Erdman" /><ref name="The Role of Modeling and Simulation in Development and Registration of Medicinal Products: Output From the EFPIA/EMA Modeling and Simulation Workshop. Manolis">{{cite journal | vauthors = Manolis E, Rohou S, Hemmings R, Salmonson T, Karlsson M, Milligan PA | title = The Role of Modeling and Simulation in Development and Registration of Medicinal Products: Output From the EFPIA/EMA Modeling and Simulation Workshop | journal =   CPT: Pharmacometrics & Systems Pharmacology| volume = 2 | issue = 2 | pages = e31 | date = February 2013 | pmid = 23835942 | pmc = 3600760 | doi = 10.1038/psp.2013.7 }}</ref> and may be able to provide information that could be used to refine the product to such a degree that it could successfully complete clinical trials.

''In silico'' clinical trials would also provide significant benefits over current pre-clinical practices. Unlike animal models, the virtual human models can be re-used indefinitely, providing significant cost savings.  Compared to trials in animals or a small sample of humans, ''in silico'' trials might more effectively predict the behaviour of the drug or device in large-scale trials, identifying side effects that were previously difficult or impossible to detect, helping to prevent unsuitable candidates from progressing to the costly phase 3 trials.<ref name="Avicenna Roadmap 2015 Viceconti" />

== In radiology ==
One relatively well-developed field of ''in-silico'' clinical trials is radiology, where the entire imaging process is digitized.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal | vauthors = Abadi E, Segars WP, Tsui BM, Kinahan PE, Bottenus N, Frangi AF, Maidment A, Lo J, Samei E | display-authors = 6 | title = Virtual clinical trials in medical imaging: a review | journal = Journal of Medical Imaging | volume = 7 | issue = 4 | article-number = 042805 | date = July 2020 | pmid = 32313817 | pmc = 7148435 | doi = 10.1117/1.JMI.7.4.042805 }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{cite book | vauthors = Maidment DA |chapter=Virtual Clinical Trials for the Assessment of Novel Breast Screening Modalities|date=2014 | title = Breast Imaging|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science|volume=8539|pages=1–8| veditors = Fujita H, Hiroshi H, Takeshi M, Muramatsu C |place=Cham|publisher=Springer International Publishing|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-07887-8_1|isbn=978-3-319-07886-1 }}</ref> The development has accelerated in recent years following the growth of computer capacity and more advanced simulation models, and is now at the point that virtual platforms are gaining acceptance by regulatory bodies as a complement to conventional clinical trials for new product introductions.<ref name=":2">{{cite journal | vauthors = Glick SJ, Ikejimba LC | title = Advances in digital and physical anthropomorphic breast phantoms for x-ray imaging | journal = Medical Physics | volume = 45 | issue = 10 | pages = e870–e885 | date = October 2018 | pmid = 30058117 | doi = 10.1002/mp.13110 | bibcode = 2018MedPh..45E.870G | s2cid = 51865533 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

A complete framework for ''in-silico'' clinical trials in radiology needs to include the following three components: 1) A realistic patient population, which is computer simulated using software phantoms; 2) The simulated response of the imaging system; 3) Image evaluation in a systematic way by human or model observers.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

Computational phantoms for imaging ''in-silico'' trials require a high degree of realism because images will be produced and evaluated. To date, the most realistic whole-body phantoms are so-called [[boundary representation]] (BREP) phantoms, which are surface representations of segmented 3D patient data (MRI or CT).<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Segars WP, Sturgeon G, Mendonca S, Grimes J, Tsui BM | title = 4D XCAT phantom for multimodality imaging research | journal = Medical Physics | volume = 37 | issue = 9 | pages = 4902–4915 | date = September 2010 | pmid = 20964209 | pmc = 2941518 | doi = 10.1118/1.3480985 | bibcode = 2010MedPh..37.4902S }}</ref> The fitted surfaces allow for modelling anatomical changes or motion in addition to realistic anatomy. Existing models for generating intra-organ structures are based on mathematical modelling, patient images, or [[generative adversarial network]] (GAN) modelling of patient images.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{cite journal|author4-link=Fang-Fang Yin | vauthors = Chang Y, Lafata K, Segars WP, Yin FF, Ren L | title = Development of realistic multi-contrast textured XCAT (MT-XCAT) phantoms using a dual-discriminator conditional-generative adversarial network (D-CGAN) | journal = Physics in Medicine and Biology | volume = 65 | issue = 6 | page = 065009 | date = March 2020 | pmid = 32023555 | pmc = 7252912 | doi = 10.1088/1361-6560/ab7309 | bibcode = 2020PMB....65f5009C }}</ref> Models of pathologies are important for simulating clinical applications targeted on specific diseases. State-of-the-art models are based on segmented lesions with enhancements for structures above the resolution limit of the imaging system using [[digital pathology]] or physiological growth models.<ref>{{Cite book| vauthors = Sauer TJ, Samei E | title = Medical Imaging 2019: Physics of Medical Imaging | chapter = Modeling dynamic, nutrient-access-based lesion progression using stochastic processes | veditors = Bosmans H, Chen GH, Gilat Schmidt T |date=2019-03-14|publisher=SPIE|volume=10948|pages=1193–1200|doi=10.1117/12.2513201|bibcode=2019SPIE10948E..50S|isbn=978-1-5106-2543-3|s2cid=92553165}}</ref> GAN models have been used to simulate disease as well.<ref>{{Cite journal| vauthors = Sauer TJ, Richards TW, Buckler AJ, Daubert M, Douglas P, Segars WP, Samei E | veditors = Bosmans H, Chen JH |date=2020-03-16|title=Synthesis of physiologically-informed computational coronary artery plaques for use in virtual clinical trials (Conference Presentation) |journal=Medical Imaging 2020: Physics of Medical Imaging|publisher=SPIE|volume=11312|pages=113121X|doi=10.1117/12.2550011|isbn=978-1-5106-3391-9|s2cid=216439674}}</ref> In addition to the above, models have been developed for organ and patient motion, blood flow and [[contrast agent]] perfusion.

The response of the imaging system is generally simulated with Monte-Carlo or raytracing system models, benchmarked to measurements on physical phantoms.<ref>{{Cite book| vauthors = Badal A, Badano A |title= 2009 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium Conference Record (NSS/MIC) |chapter= Monte Carlo simulation of X-ray imaging using a graphics processing unit |date= October 2009 |pages=4081–4084|doi=10.1109/NSSMIC.2009.5402382|isbn= 978-1-4244-3961-4 |s2cid= 9960455 |chapter-url= https://zenodo.org/record/1277481 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = di Franco F, Sarno A, Mettivier G, Hernandez AM, Bliznakova K, Boone JM, Russo P | title = GEANT4 Monte Carlo simulations for virtual clinical trials in breast X-ray imaging: Proof of concept | language = English | journal = Physica Medica | volume = 74 | pages = 133–142 | date = June 2020 | pmid = 32470909 | doi = 10.1016/j.ejmp.2020.05.007 | s2cid = 219105424 }}</ref> Medical imaging has a long history of system simulation for technology development and proprietary as well as public-domain models exist for a wide range of imaging systems.

The final step of an imaging ''in-silico'' trial is evaluation and interpretation of the generated images in a systematic way. The images can be evaluated by humans in ways similar to a conventional clinical trial, but for an ''in-silico'' trial to be really effective, image interpretation as well needs to be automized. For detection and quantification tasks, so-called observer models have been thoroughly studied and validated against human observers, and a range of spatial-domain models exist in the literature.<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Abbey CK, Barrett HH | title = Human- and model-observer performance in ramp-spectrum noise: effects of regularization and object variability | language = EN | journal = Journal of the Optical Society of America A | volume = 18 | issue = 3 | pages = 473–488 | date = March 2001 | pmid = 11265678 | doi = 10.1364/JOSAA.18.000473 | pmc = 2943344 | bibcode = 2001JOSAA..18..473A }}</ref> Image interpretation based on [[deep learning]] and artificial intelligence (AI) is an active research field,<ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Rajkomar A, Dean J, Kohane I | title = Machine Learning in Medicine | journal = The New England Journal of Medicine | volume = 380 | issue = 14 | pages = 1347–1358 | date = April 2019 | pmid = 30943338 | doi = 10.1056/NEJMra1814259 | s2cid = 92996321 }}</ref> and might become a valuable aid for the radiologist to find abnormalities or to make decisions. Applying AI observers in ''in-silico'' trials is relatively straightforward as the entire image chain is digitized.
